data.title: Hong Kong’s yacht industry eyes mainland China buyers but challenges remain
data.description:
Hong Kong’s yacht industry is seeking to attract more buyers and visitors from mainland China under a new cross-boundary travel scheme, but relatively high berthing costs could pose a challenge, industry representatives have said.
Industry leaders, exhibitors and visitors gathered in Discovery Bay on Friday for the fourth edition of the Lantau Yacht Club Boat Show, which runs until Sunday.
The show featured more than 30 vessels, including superyachts and models from international brands such as Sunseeker, Princess and Azimut.
The Southbound Yacht Travel Scheme, which allows eligible Guangdong-registered yachts to sail into Hong Kong waters, was launched last month as part of Hong Kong’s broader efforts to develop its yacht economy.
Franklin Mak, executive vice-president of hospitality at HKR International, the developer behind the Lantau Yacht Club, said the yacht economy extended beyond vessel sales to include tourism, hospitality and related services.

Tommy Ho, chairman of the Hong Kong Yachting Association, estimated that mainland buyers could account for about 200 additional yacht purchases in Hong Kong under the new scheme, while local demand was expected to remain steady.
Ho said his organisation had recently received a growing number of inquiries from mainland yacht enthusiasts interested in visiting the city, including requests for sailing routes and tourist destinations.
Liao Kai, chairman of the Zhuhai Yacht Association, said the new arrangement was also expected to strengthen links between Hong Kong’s yacht services and Zhuhai, which was a major yacht production centre.
While Hong Kong could offer mainland buyers a wider choice of international brands and quality second-hand vessels, Liao said the city’s relatively higher prices of yachts compared with the mainland could make it less attractive.
Bryan Van Dale, an international yacht-equipment supplier, said the main downside of Hong Kong’s boat business was that moorings were too expensive and in short supply.

data.title: More funding could be sought if HK$10b university town loan scheme falls short
data.description:
Hong Kong’s education secretary has said she will seek additional funding if a HK$10 billion loan scheme falls short of the needs of institutions setting foot in the Northern Metropolis’ first university town, while warning that their financial plans must be feasible and they must not “take chances”.
A task force jointly established by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority and the Hong Kong Association of Banks will designate 11 tertiary institutions as public sector entities to help them secure bank financing for projects in the Northern Metropolis.
Secretary for Education Christine Choi Yuk-lin told a Legislative Council panel meeting on Friday that institutions seeking to establish themselves in the university towns, as well as lawmakers, had called for more financial support.
She also told some media outlets that she would seek additional funding from the financial secretary if institutions approved to set foot in the first university town needed more than the HK$10 billion earmarked for loans.
“In addition to the government loan, we will encourage and line up different government departments to form platforms to let institutions present their development proposals to some potential investors to secure flexible financing,” she told the education panel meeting.




The government plans to develop three self-financed university towns, with a core campus area totalling 300 hectares, in the Northern Metropolis megaproject near the border with mainland China, fostering collaboration among industry, academia and the research sector.
Three university towns are planned: the 26-hectare Hung Shui Kiu university town; the 100-hectare San Tin university town; and the 180-hectare Ta Kwu Ling university town. The government earmarked a HK$10 billion loan scheme for the first one, Hung Shui Kiu university town.
The Hung Shui Kiu town and its adjoining technology and industry areas will be developed as a “centre for applied post-secondary education in smart manufacturing and global talent cultivation”.
Institutions wishing to establish a presence in Hung Shui Kiu must submit their proposals by the end of next month, with the government expected to announce the successful bids early next year.
Choi said institutions had to secure funding from diverse sources, as existing rules stipulated that the government loans could not exceed 50 per cent of project costs. She warned that the institutions had to formulate a feasible financial plan to repay the loans.
She said the Designated Vetting Group, led by the chief secretary, would review the institutions’ proposals and assess their financing arrangements to see if they were feasible.
“We will not tolerate any situation where an institution suddenly finds itself unable to repay its debts. Therefore, institutions must not rely on wishful thinking or take chances during their planning,” she said.
At a meeting of Legco’s financial affairs panel, Arthur Yuen Kwok-hang, deputy chief executive of the Monetary Authority, said the Northern Metropolis Financial Advisory Taskforce, set up in April, would discuss ways to help universities secure loans from banks at its next meeting.
The task force was set up to explore financing solutions to support the development of the Northern Metropolis.
Yuen said the authority would list nine universities and two post-secondary colleges as public sector entities in its Banking (Capital) Rules.
“It will make it considerably easier for them to secure financing solutions when carrying out developments in the university towns,” he said.

Lawmaker Andrew Yao Cho-fai, council chairman of Lingnan University, welcomed the move and said his institution was preparing a proposal for the Hung Shui Kiu project.
“This is a very promising start … because our primary concern is funding. Aside from borrowing from the government, we hope to secure more financing from commercial banks,” he said.
The government previously said the Hung Shui Kiu university town had three plots, each with a maximum plot ratio of five.
The largest site covers 165,200 square metres and can yield 826,000 square metres of total floor space, with the plot to be handed over in stages from 2026 to 2029.
The second covers 52,800 square metres, with 264,000 square metres of floor space. The handover is scheduled between 2027 and 2029.
The smallest is 43,700 square metres, allowing 218,500 square metres of floor space under a 110-metre height limit, with the site handover scheduled for 2027.

data.title: Hong Kong firms must innovate to compete in mainland China, trade chief says
data.description:
Hong Kong companies can survive intense competition in mainland China by being innovative and maintaining high standards, the head of the city’s trade promotion body has said.
Hong Kong Trade Development Council chairman Frederick Ma Si-hang said on Friday that the city was also tapping into emerging markets in Southeast Asia, the Middle East and Africa to counter global trade uncertainties.
“I feel that Hong Kong manufacturers need to be more innovative; think of ways to use our strengths to penetrate this huge mainland consumer market,” he said.
“We need to know what their tastes are before we can penetrate this market.”
Ma was speaking on the sidelines of the ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE) in Shanghai, which has attracted more than 400 Hong Kong exhibitors this year.
He said businesses should capitalise on Hong Kong’s unique advantages, including the “one country, two systems” governing principle. The city’s professional services providers could also use their expertise to help mainland companies expand globally.
He added that Hong Kong was exploring emerging markets to counter global trade uncertainties following the elections in the United States.
“We have seen that many emerging markets are actually giving Hong Kong a lot of momentum, and growth is relatively strong,” he said.
“While we must take care of our traditional markets on one hand, on the other hand, we are also exploring some emerging markets, such as Central Asia, the Middle East and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.”
Ma said the council would open an office in Egypt next year to expand its promotional network in Africa amid geopolitical shifts.

He added that Hong Kong was catching up fast in innovation and technology, which would allow closer cooperation with the mainland.
“The artificial intelligence trend will not stop, and there is a trend that China’s development might be faster than the United States,” he said.
Ma cited views that the US election results could slow the country’s technological progress while China continued to advance rapidly.
He also expressed hope that Hong Kong would overtake London in global financial centre rankings next year. He pointed to what he described as the city’s achievement in surpassing Switzerland in wealth management, saying this was “not simple”.
Standard Chartered’s CEO for Hong Kong, Greater China and North Asia, Mary Huen Wai-yee, said the Shanghai expo highlighted the Chinese market’s immense potential.
She added that the bank was helping businesses connect with the world as China continued to open its market.
“This year, Standard Chartered continues to act as a superconnector, showcasing innovative results in areas such as cross-border trade, wealth management and sustainable finance, using the power of finance to connect China and the world,” she said.
“The import expo allows the world to share the dividends of China’s development and also shows the huge potential of the Chinese market.”

data.title: Crypto heavyweight eyes Hong Kong expansion to tap growing tokenisation demand
data.description:
Solana, one of the world’s largest blockchain networks, plans to expand in Hong Kong to tap the city’s growing demand for tokenisation, according to a senior executive.
“I believe that the biggest opportunity for Solana is actually in [the Asia-Pacific region],” Solana Company chairman and CEO Joseph Chee said in an interview in Hong Kong earlier this week.
Founded in the US in 2018, the company is behind one of the most popular cryptocurrencies. With a market capitalisation of about US$53 billion on Friday, the Solana token was the world’s seventh-largest cryptocurrency, according to CoinMarketCap.
The Solana Foundation was established in 2020 to maintain the blockchain network bearing its name, while Nasdaq-listed Solana Company focused on “acquiring and holding” its tokens and “offering public market investors direct exposure to Solana”, according to a December filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission.
In Hong Kong, Solana Company had positioned itself as a digital asset infrastructure and service provider, the firm said last month after being named a “strategic enterprise” by the city government’s Office for Attracting Strategic Enterprises.
The company said it planned to use its Hong Kong operation, which also serves as its new Asia-Pacific headquarters, to explore how digital asset infrastructure could “contribute to the city’s financial institutions”.

Hong Kong has identified tokenisation as a key area of fintech development, with a growing number of firms launching blockchain-based financial products.
Julia Leung Fung-yee, CEO of the Securities and Futures Commission, said at the annual Hong Kong FinTech Week earlier this week that regulators had authorised 17 tokenised retail products with total assets under management of US$1.3 billion, up 34 per cent from a year earlier.
Still, the US was “moving a lot faster” in tokenisation, Chee said.
“A lot of major financial institutions in Hong Kong are just starting to think about or initiate a [tokenisation] project,” he said, adding that the company expected to have “a good sense of where Hong Kong is” within about six months.
Solana Company aimed to grow its Hong Kong team to as many as 30 employees from fewer than 10 currently, according to Chee. If no major tokenisation service providers emerged in the city within the next six months, “we might just build a team” to meet demand from local banks, he said.

data.title: Hong Kong authorities arrest 28 in crackdown on bid-rigging after Tai Po fire
data.description:
Hong Kong authorities have cracked down on a bid-rigging syndicate and arrested 28 people, including directors of contractors and consultancy firms as well as some with triad backgrounds, in the first operation by a joint task force after the devastating Wang Fuk Court fire.
Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung said on Friday that the task force, formed to combat bid-rigging, had also set up a 24-hour hotline for the public to report any suspected bid-rigging activities and would offer monetary rewards in appropriate circumstances.
The arrests are the first since a damning report on the deadly Tai Po blaze by an independent committee was released last week.
Tang told a press conference that the government had taken action after discovering a triad-related bid-rigging group was pushing through deals before more measures came into effect.
“They hoped to ‘take the last bus’ and used excuses such as price fluctuations of materials, urgency to start the projects, to trick owners to quickly sign the contracts, and so they could choose the project consultants and contractors of the syndicate,” Tang said.
“They hoped to seek exorbitant profits at the last minute.”
Those arrested included managing directors and staff members from six contractors, 10 consultancy firms, one property management company and one owners’ corporation.
Some of them had triad backgrounds, Tang said.
He said the group had obtained 12 contracts for building projects across Hong Kong, involving about HK$100 million (US$12.7 million), using illegal means such as coercion, bribery and blackmail.
Senior officials from the Independent Commission Against Corruption and the Competition Commission also attended the press conference.
The joint task force – involving police, the Independent Commission Against Corruption and the Competition Commission – was set up to combat crimes related to bid-rigging in maintenance projects following the release of the committee’s report.
The housing estate was undergoing large-scale renovation works when the blaze broke out last November, killing 168 people.
The government also announced last week that it was set to criminalise bid-rigging in building maintenance projects under laws covering triad and corruption offences and allow authorities to take criminal or civil action against such conduct.
The change will introduce a criminal offence with penalties of up to 10 years’ imprisonment and fines.
According to the committee’s report, bid-rigging and associated misconduct may involve multiple parties such as building contractors, consultants, property management companies, middlemen, building management committee members and even homeowners, with some of them having triad affiliations.
The committee said that while it was not within its scope to determine whether there had been bid-rigging in the Wang Fuk Court case, there were “numerous features of that project which bore the hallmarks of bid-rigging and anti-competitive conduct”.

data.title: China’s AI chipmakers report first profits, but will the trend continue?
data.description:
China’s pure-play artificial intelligence chipmakers crossed an important milestone in the third quarter as several firms swung into profit, but severe supply chain hurdles and soaring memory costs cloud their long-term growth prospects.
Domestic graphics processing unit (GPU) developers including Moore Threads, MetaX and Iluvatar CoreX are racing to fill the market void left by Nvidia, whose high-end processors face strict US export controls.
These home-grown firms are competing fiercely to win over domestic enterprise clients and penetrate major cloud service providers (CSPs).
Beijing-based Moore Threads, one of the “four little dragons” in China’s GPU space, led the earnings turnaround, posting an adjusted net profit of 49.26 million yuan (US$7.4 million) for the quarter, driven by a 1,774 per cent year-on-year surge in revenue. It was the chipmaker’s first profitable quarter.
Shanghai-based MetaX recorded a net profit of 26.5 million yuan, marking its second profitable quarter of the year.
The momentum faces headwinds, however. The domestic sector is grappling with an acute shortage of high-bandwidth memory (HBM), an indispensable component in the systems for training and running large AI models.
As US export controls reduced supply, factory prices for 36GB HBM3e modules skyrocketed to more than US$4,000 on grey markets from around US$500 before the memory squeeze, according to recent supply-chain checks by Morgan Stanley.
The cost surge threatens the margins that enabled the chipmakers’ early profits. Moore Threads’ gross margin contracted by more than 8 percentage points year on year in the first three quarters as it stockpiled expensive components.
For MetaX, another little dragon, limited scale among tier-one CSPs makes absorbing these spikes even harder, despite raising prices for its flagship C600 processor, according to Morgan Stanley, which has lowered its 2027 and 2028 gross margin forecasts for the chipmaker.

The industry’s challenges extend beyond memory pricing to production and adoption delays.
Although MetaX secured an order for around 20,000 units of its C600A variant from e-commerce giant JD.com, Morgan Stanley said that this provided “insufficient evidence of broader hyperscaler adoption”, leaving the company reliant on government and regional computing projects.
MetaX’s Xiyun C600, which entered mass production earlier this year, pairs HBM3e memory with a precision architecture suited to model training.
Volume shipments for MetaX’s next-generation C700 processor could also be delayed until late 2027, risking a critical window to win over enterprise accounts, the bank said.
Meanwhile, hardware rivalry is intensifying. Last month, Shanghai-based Iluvatar CoreX held a live demonstration of its new Tiangai 300 GPU, claiming it matched or even outperformed Nvidia’s H200 in real-world AI workloads.
Chipmakers focused on application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) rather than GPUs also face operational strains.
Cambricon Technologies, widely seen as one of China’s leading alternatives to foreign AI hardware suppliers, is grappling with the financial weight of securing its supply chain.
The company’s inventory surged by 3.42 billion yuan quarter-on-quarter to 11.6 billion yuan at the end of September, leading to an inventory impairment loss of 502 million yuan over the first nine months of the year.
Even so, Cambricon has quickly penetrated mainstream cloud infrastructure. Having delivered its MLU692 chip to a major CSP for testing in the third quarter, the company was projected by Morgan Stanley to ship nearly 350,000 units to CSP clients next year alongside the roll-out of its next-generation MLU580.
In a recent research note, Goldman Sachs analysts said long-term survival for Chinese AI chipmakers would hinge on sustaining profitability while improving local fabrication capacity and production yields.
Despite immediate supply challenges, Nomura analysts argued in a report last month that financial markets continued to underestimate “both the breadth of AI demand and the earnings that such strong demand can generate across the value chain”.
They added that sustained cuts to computing commitments or significant delays to funded projects would challenge that outlook.

data.title: Hong Kong temperatures to fall to 18 degrees next week as cold front hits
data.description:
Temperatures in Hong Kong are expected to drop to as low as 18 degrees Celsius (64.4 Fahrenheit) on Tuesday as a cold front hits the city early next week.
According to the Hong Kong Observatory, a strong monsoon over the weekend will bring cooler weather.
“A strong northeast monsoon will affect the coast of Guangdong over the weekend. A cold front is expected to move across the coast of southern China at first on Monday,” the forecaster said on Friday.
“Under the influence of the associated intense northeast monsoon, winds will strengthen from the north and temperatures will fall appreciably over the region.”
The forecaster’s nine-day forecast shows temperatures will stand between 25 and 29 degrees over the weekend, before dipping significantly to as low as 20 degrees on Monday and 18 degrees on Tuesday. Minimum temperatures will then gradually rise to around 24 degrees next weekend.
The weather will be generally fine and dry over Guangdong province in the middle of next week. It will be cool in the morning over inland areas, and the temperature difference between day and night will be relatively large.
Upper-air disturbances are expected to bring rainy weather to southern China next weekend.

data.title: HKEX posts first quarterly profit decline in over 2 years as market cools
data.description:
Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX), the operator of Asia’s third-largest stock market, has reported its first year-on-year decline in quarterly profit in over two years amid a slowdown in market turnover, with profits falling 10 per cent compared with the previous quarter.
Net profit for the three months to September fell 1 per cent year on year to HK$4.859 billion (US$620 million), or HK$3.84 per share, missing analysts’ estimates of HK$5 billion, according to an exchange filing on Friday.
This marked the exchange operator’s first year-on-year drop in quarterly profit in 10 quarters, trailing the HK$5.4 billion recorded in the second quarter and HK$5.2 billion in the first.
Its total profit for the first three quarters stood at a record high of HK$15.4 billion, up 15 per cent from a year earlier and matching market expectations.
“As we navigate heightened macro uncertainties and ongoing volatility, our conviction in building a deeper and more diverse multi-asset ecosystem has only strengthened,” said Bonnie Chan Yiting, CEO of HKEX.
“The sustained momentum reflected in our latest set of results shows the resilience of our business and reinforces our confidence in the long-term growth and competitiveness of Hong Kong’s markets.”
The share price of HKEX fell as much as 3 per cent Friday afternoon after reporting its first quarterly decline in two years, and closed 2.2 per cent lower on Friday at HK$385.6, while the broader Hang Seng Index fell 1.2 per cent.
The decline in profit was driven by an 8 per cent rise in operating expenses, attributable to higher staff and information technology costs.
Total revenue for the third quarter stood at HK$7.86 billion, slightly lower than market estimates of HK$8 billion.




The flat performance was driven by an 11 per cent year-on-year drop in average daily turnover on the securities market during the quarter. For the first nine months of the year, the average daily turnover was up 6 per cent year on year at HK$272.9 billion, according to exchange data.
There was a 2.5 per cent decrease in trading fees for the third quarter due to lower market turnover. The decline in trading fees was largely offset by higher listing fees and stronger commodities and northbound trading, the exchange said.
The decline was also offset by a 39 per cent jump in investment income to HK$353 million. This was a result of higher investment returns during the three-month period, and the absence of last year’s foreign exchange losses from a weaker US dollar.
The benchmark Hang Seng Index has fallen 4.5 per cent so far this year, making it one of the world’s worst-performing benchmarks.
Listing fees also rose 35 per cent for the first three quarters, a result of an increase in new listings. The first three quarters saw 118 initial public offerings that raised a combined HK$388 billion, 106 per cent higher than a year earlier.
However, momentum showed signs of cooling as trading entered the fourth quarter. The latest HKEX data reveals that average daily turnover slipped to HK$180.7 billion in October, well below the 10-month average of HK$263.8 billion.
The Wall Street investment bank Citibank said in a research note on Friday it believed the current consensus may not have fully factored in the weak trading volume in September and expected a relatively muted share price reaction, as HKEX’s weak share price performance in recent months could have largely reflected expectations of softer trading activities.
While IPO proceeds surged 84 per cent year-on-year to HK$403.9 billion in the first 10 months with 121 new listings, market sentiment has picked up further as the Hang Seng Index rebounded alongside trading volumes recently, said Nip Chun-pong, chief financial analyst at Solo Securities.
“Supported by this momentum and a warming IPO pipeline, HKEX’s fourth-quarter and full-year earnings are expected to remain solid,” he added.

data.title: Does the Democratic midterm victory spell the end of US AI data centre boom?
data.description:
The sweeping midterm election victory by US Democrats has triggered warnings from analysts that an impending regulatory clampdown could derail the nation’s multi-trillion-dollar artificial intelligence data centre buildout.
Wall Street forecasters slashed their projections for Big Tech infrastructure spending hours after the vote, cautioning that a wave of proposed project moratoria and tighter oversight could stall up to 30 per cent of planned US facilities and force developers to downscale their capacity plans.
The pessimism sent shock waves through equities on Thursday US time.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 plunged more than 6.3 per cent, wiping out US$2.3 trillion in market capitalisation, while the broader S&P 500 tumbled 4.4 per cent, erasing US$2.8 trillion. It marked the worst day for both benchmarks since April 2025, when global tariffs under US President Donald Trump sent world markets into turmoil.
Market sentiment on the breakneck buildout of US AI data centres, which had enjoyed strong support under the Trump administration, deteriorated almost overnight as political headwinds shifted in key states.
Texas emerged as ground zero for investor anxiety following the victory of Democratic Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, who pledged an immediate freeze on approvals for new data centres until state authorities address mounting concerns over surging electricity tariffs, water consumption and impact on local communities.

Compounding Wall Street’s unease, newly elected progressives in Washington quickly signalled plans for federal intervention.
Less than 24 hours after Democrats recaptured majorities in both chambers of Congress, US Representative Yassamin Ansari of Arizona publicly urged a pause on advanced AI development, stricter oversight of the industry and a ban on artificial superintelligence.
The political shift across the country prompted financial institutions to aggressively downgrade their growth forecasts for domestic AI facilities.
Analysts at US investment bank Yorkville Ives said they now expected Big Tech capital expenditure growth to peak in 2027, ahead of previous projections of 2028 or 2029.
“While Big Tech and hyperscaler capex should still easily exceed US$1 trillion in 2027, the growth rate into 2028 will clearly moderate significantly as the data centre buildout comes at a much slower pace given the political map, especially in the state of Texas,” the bank said in a research note.
Yorkville Ives projected that of the 800 to 1,000 AI data centre projects currently planned nationwide, at least 10 per cent faced cancellation, while another 20 per cent could encounter prolonged regulatory delays.
Industry experts warned that a protracted pause on utility-scale facilities would ripple across the entire tech ecosystem.
Felix Wang, managing director and global tech sector head at Hedgeye, described the rout as “very bad for AI names”, warning that bottlenecks in major hubs could force frontier developers such as OpenAI and Anthropic to turn to smaller 20-to-30 megawatt facilities.
Wang added that the regulatory overhang could potentially delay Anthropic’s planned public debut from this month until next year, amid speculation that its valuation could be lowered to between US$1 trillion and US$1.25 trillion.
Wall Street trading desks reported intense, one-sided selling throughout the day.

John Flood, head of Americas equity execution services at Goldman Sachs, told clients the desk saw an abrupt reversal from Wednesday’s frantic activity, with phones “exploding” from investors seeking guidance but almost no willing buyers stepping in.
The sell-off was especially brutal across the hardware supply chain powering the AI data-centre buildout. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index tumbled 12 per cent. Nvidia lost more than 9 per cent, while Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) plunged over 17 per cent.
Entities closely linked to tech billionaire Elon Musk were also hit. Shares of SpaceX and Tesla tumbled by more than 9 per cent and nearly 11 per cent, respectively, wiping more than US$300 billion off their combined market values on Thursday.
Musk had injected nearly US$450 million into Republican campaigns during the midterms, including heavy backing for Ken Paxton’s failed US Senate bid in Texas.
Trump swiftly took to Truth Social to blame the crash on the election outcome.
“The Stock Market suffered one of the worst days in History based on the results of the Election. Such a sad thing to watch!” Trump wrote.
“It took so much work to get us to a level that no one has ever seen before, and then this. Your 401(k)s have, therefore, dropped. Remember, it wasn’t Republicans, it was Dumocrats.”
Additional reporting by Vincent Chow

data.title: 5 months’ jail for helper convicted of molesting employer’s 12-year-old daughter
data.description:
A Hong Kong court has sentenced a domestic helper to five months in jail for molesting her former employer’s 12-year-old daughter in the family home.
Lady Jay Santos Flores, 45, offered no mitigation before she was sentenced at Kowloon City Court on Friday on three counts of indecent assault. She sobbed occasionally during the hearing.
Flores was convicted last month of molesting the girl, who said the Filipino helper had touched her genitals on several occasions between May and June 2025.
The girl’s younger sister, who was 10 at the time, also accused Flores of stroking her buttocks several times on the morning of June 11, 2025, when the helper entered her room to wake her.
The younger girl told her sister what had happened and learnt that the older girl had experienced similar treatment.
At the time of the incidents, Flores had worked for the family for about six months and shared a room with the older sister.
Magistrate Claudia Ng Cheuk-hwa convicted Flores of three counts of indecent assault involving the older girl, ruling that the physical contact was intentional and indecent.
But Ng acquitted the helper of the charge involving the younger sister, finding that the touching could have been accidental.
At Friday’s hearing, Ng said the offences involved a breach of trust and an assault on a minor.
The magistrate noted that the older girl had declined an assessment by healthcare professionals for an impact report.
When the sisters told their mother about the incidents, she suggested letting the matter go.
But the older girl spoke to staff at her school, which later contacted police.

data.title: As political bet fails, what happens now to Musk’s Tesla, SpaceX and China ties?
data.description:
Elon Musk bet nearly half a billion dollars that political spending could keep Washington friendly to his sprawling business empire. On Tuesday, that bet came up short.
As Democrats recaptured control of the US Congress in the midterm elections, the world’s richest man found himself facing an abruptly altered political landscape.
After pouring a record-breaking US$474 million into political groups – overwhelmingly backing Republicans – Musk now faces a divided Washington keen to examine his sprawling web of domestic government contracts and deep commercial links to China.
The political shift threatens to complicate operations across Musk’s corporate universe just as his enterprises, from Tesla and SpaceX to xAI, have become deeply intertwined with both Washington and Beijing.
Markets reacted swiftly on Wednesday morning. SpaceX shares fell 4 per cent and Tesla tumbled 5 per cent shortly after the opening bell.




Musk attempted to laugh off the setback on social media, writing: “Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time.”
He said in another post: “Data centres in space looking pretty appealing right now.”
Behind the bravado, billions of dollars are on the line. Under US President Donald Trump’s second administration, Musk’s ventures flourished on the back of major federal contracts and swift regulatory approvals.
Since stepping down from his controversial post heading the Department of Government Efficiency (Doge) in May 2025, his companies had secured at least US$10 billion in new federal deals, according to an October report by the Democracy Defenders Fund, a non-profit watchdog.
Nowhere is the scrutiny expected to bite harder than at SpaceX, whose role as a major defence contractor makes it a particularly obvious target for congressional oversight.
Democrats … want to examine Musk’s government contracts and potential conflicts of interest involving SpaceX and Tesla
Christopher Tang, University of California, Los Angeles
In May alone, SpaceX won two US Space Force contracts worth a combined US$6.45 billion, including a US$4.16 billion agreement to develop satellites capable of tracking airborne threats.
Meanwhile, his AI venture, xAI, landed a nearly US$200 million Department of Defence contract in July 2025.
“The new Democrat-controlled Congress will likely diminish Musk’s influence in Washington to some extent, although he still seems to have Trump’s ear,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution.
Chan noted that lawmakers could investigate SpaceX’s military deals as well as Musk’s conduct during his tenure at Doge, including allegations concerning the misuse of government data.
The Shanghai question
A key flashpoint on Capitol Hill is the intersection of Musk’s defence portfolio and Tesla’s extensive reliance on China.
Tesla’s Shanghai Gigafactory accounted for more than half of the company’s global vehicle deliveries last year, while production elsewhere depends on a network of Chinese suppliers.
The company also produces energy-storage batteries in Shanghai and has been in talks to buy nearly US$3 billion of Chinese solar manufacturing equipment to support its US expansion.
Musk’s recent hints at merging Tesla and SpaceX – announcing in October that the firms had formed special committees to explore a merger – could hand lawmakers an immediate opening.
“Democrats have already said they want to examine Musk’s government contracts and potential conflicts of interest involving SpaceX and Tesla, so expect Shanghai to be framed as a security question rather than a cost advantage,” said Christopher Tang, a professor specialising in global supply chains at the Anderson School of Management at the University of California, Los Angeles.
Any merger review is expected to examine whether sensitive aerospace and defence technology could remain effectively insulated from Tesla’s Chinese supply chain.
“Washington controls contracts and clearances, while Beijing controls inputs, cost and speed,” Tang said. “The election tightened the Washington side of that vice without loosening the Beijing side.”


Trouble on the home turf
Musk’s electoral setback was felt just as keenly in Texas, the de facto operational nerve centre of his empire.
He funnelled US$224 million into Texas races – nearly half of his overall midterm war chest – according to a CNBC analysis of campaign finance records. That did not stop Democrat Gina Hinojosa from ousting Republican incumbent Greg Abbott in the gubernatorial contest.
“The backlash over data centres has spread across the country, and some candidates made it a big part of their campaigns,” said Daniel Kollar, deputy managing director for Greater China at consultancy Intralink.
Hinojosa campaigned on freezing approvals for new data centres until environmental and energy safeguards were established, tapping into grassroots frustration over surging electricity bills and water usage.
While such restrictions would not halt existing operations at Tesla’s Austin Gigafactory, SpaceX’s Starbase in Boca Chica, or a planned joint semiconductor facility, they could complicate Musk’s ambitions to build out AI infrastructure in the region.
Ahead of its initial public offering in June, SpaceX pitched AI computing as a cornerstone of its future growth, citing an estimated US$28.5 trillion addressable market.
Congress can make Shanghai politically more expensive. It cannot make it less productive
Christopher Tang, University of California, Los Angeles
Resilience in China
Despite the political headwinds, analysts said Tesla’s Chinese production was unlikely to buckle under US congressional pressure.
Beyond vehicle assembly, Chinese suppliers play a critical role in Musk’s long-term robotics vision.
Tesla engineers audited Chinese component makers including Zhejiang Sanhua Intelligent Controls, Ningbo Joyson Electronic and Tuopu Group ahead of planned mass production of its Optimus humanoid robot, the South China Morning Post reported in September.
“Congress can make Shanghai politically more expensive. It cannot make it less productive,” Tang said.
“Given how many US companies still do business in China and rely heavily on Chinese suppliers, I think Congress would have a hard time explaining why it was singling out Tesla,” Kollar said.
Bai Wenxi, chief economist at China Enterprise Capital Union, expressed a similar view. “Tesla’s China operations won’t grind to a halt just because Musk faces investigations,” Bai said.


Sidelined in diplomacy
Where Musk may lose influence, however, was in his role as an informal intermediary between Beijing and Washington, analysts said.
Over the past year, some observers viewed Musk as a potential backchannel between the two governments. He joined Trump’s delegation to Beijing in May and secured a seat at the head table during the White House state dinner for President Xi Jinping in September.
That role had become increasingly irrelevant following the US-China trade truce reached in South Korea last year, according to Brookings Institution’s Chan.
“At the start of Trump’s second term, many wondered whether Elon Musk would play a moderating role in the White House’s approach to China,” Chan said. “After the Busan agreement, there seems to be less of a role for someone like Musk to play in US-China relations.”
Bai said Musk’s value as a diplomatic conduit had diminished.
“Musk himself has gone from being a ‘strategic bridge’ to just one of the American businessmen Beijing can engage with,” he said.
Ultimately, however, Trump remains in the Oval Office for the next two years, holding executive veto power and agency leadership that could shield Musk from major regulatory challenges. But the days of unfettered access may be over.
“My guess is Musk will keep a lower political profile for a while to draw less attention to his businesses,” Kollar said.
“There will likely be increased congressional scrutiny, but without executive action, I’d be surprised if he changed his merger plans or how Tesla operates in China.”

data.title: Hong Kong privacy watchdog backs tighter rules on access to land records
data.description:
Hong Kong’s privacy watchdog has backed a proposed overhaul of rules to tighten access to land records, warning that journalists have no exemption when collecting data as complaints over information misuse appear to be worsening.
Privacy Commissioner Ada Chung Lai-ling said on Friday that journalists do not enjoy an exemption under the Privacy Ordinance when gathering information, even though certain safeguards apply to how the data is subsequently used.
“The Privacy Ordinance does provide an exemption on the use of personal data for journalistic activities, which means journalists do not need the prior consent of the data subject before publishing or broadcasting the relevant data. However, the prerequisite is that the publication or broadcast must be in the public interest,” she told a radio programme.
“This aligns completely with the rationale under the currently proposed new arrangement, where conducting searches must serve the public interest … I would also like to point out that under Section 61 of the Privacy Ordinance, there is no exemption whatsoever for media practitioners when it comes to the collection of data.”
She said data collection must be done lawfully, citing an instance of media professionals using telephoto lenses to observe the conditions inside an individual’s home, which does not enjoy any exemption under the Privacy Ordinance.
Chung said the watchdog received 20 complaints of misusing information obtained from the land register over the past five years, six of which were made this year, showing signs of a worsening situation.
Examples of misusing personal data included doxxing and direct marketing. In some cases, owners’ information was uploaded onto social media platforms due to financial disputes.
“If you compare the number of complaints against the total volume of searches, it does not seem like that many. I believe that the vast majority are law-abiding,” she said.
“We have seen cases where information from the land register was disclosed online, or even cyberbullying and doxxing – not even one of those cases should happen.”
Chung said it was “not ideal” that people conducting land searches were not required to stipulate the purpose for obtaining the information.
She explained that requiring people to specify the purpose not only allows the department to run the system smoothly but also protects people who conduct land searches because they would know the data could only be used for this specific purpose, but not any other – which could be a violation of the privacy ordinance.
“Therefore, from a data protection perspective, the proposal would enhance the clarity of the land search system, strengthen the protection of owners’ personal data … while offering convenience to the operation of the system and protecting those conducting land searches from falling foul of the law. This is a win-win-win situation.”
The government earlier tabled eight pieces of subsidiary legislation, including the Land Titles Regulation that covers land record search arrangements, at the Legislative Council for negative vetting.
Under the new regime, land record searches providing essential details – such as owner identities, purchase prices and registration dates – are restricted to nine specific purposes.
The specific purposes include property valuation, due diligence for transactions, building management, legal proceedings, conducting academic and market research and conducting inspections in the public interest.
Applications citing the public interest will be reviewed case-by-case, considering how the records would be used to serve the interests of society, whether they outweigh the right to privacy and whether the documents would be misused, among other factors.
A development official said earlier that the government would strive to minimise inconvenience to the media by lowering the threshold for requests and replying within one to two days, in a bid to reduce the chance of outlets objecting to the decisions made by the registrar.

data.title: Breaking|12½ years’ jail for ex-Macau lawmaker in city’s first national security trial
data.description:
Former Macau lawmaker Au Kam-san has been convicted on five out of seven charges in the city’s first national security trial, with the court handing him a 12½-year prison sentence.
The Court of First Instance in Macau on Friday found the 69-year-old guilty on four counts under the city’s national security law – subversion of state power and establishing links with foreign groups or individuals to commit activities endangering national security – as well as a fifth count of violation of secrecy.
The court acquitted Au of two counts of subversion of state power that arose from his alleged collusion with multiple foreign organisations, according to a court press release.
In a statement released soon after the verdict, a Macau government spokesman said that the city’s court had reached its judgment in accordance with the law and protected the defendant’s rights.
“The [Macau] government urges society to respect the court’s judgment and support the judiciary’s exercise of its right to judge, defending the tradition of judicial justice and the rule of law,” he said.
The trial, the first in Macau since the casino hub enacted its domestic national security law in 2009, was held behind closed doors in September and concluded in just two days.
Ahead of the public verdict hearing on Friday morning, Macau authorities published a press release announcing gallery seating arrangements for the public and media on Thursday afternoon. Media registration lasted for about an hour until 4pm that day.
A South China Morning Post reporter inquired about the availability of public gallery tickets at the Court of First Instance on Friday morning and was told they had been “snapped up in a few minutes” the day before.
“We already tried to offer more seats than usual, but we cannot accommodate 100, or 200 people. Our seats are very limited,” a court staff member said.
Another staff member from the Macau government’s press office told the SCMP that only four seats were available to media on a first-come, first-served basis. They were taken by local outlets: the Chinese and Portuguese channels of broadcaster Teledifusao de Macau, and the broadsheets Macau Daily News and Tai Chung Daily.
It was quiet outside the court building on Friday morning, with the SCMP observing fewer than 20 people entering the premises before the hearing’s scheduled 10am start time.
At 9am, around 10 police officers, including both uniformed and plainclothes officers, stood guard at junctions and pedestrian paths leading to the court entrance.
Police also blocked off nearby junctions, with cars prohibited from stopping in the area.
A prison van entered the court building at 9.38am. A prison van was again spotted departing the court building at 11.15am, after details of Au’s sentence were published online.
In a public letter, Au’s wife Virginia Cheang Mio-san wrote that the national security trial was an act of “political persecution” against her husband and that the family would not accept the sentence.
“From a closed door trial to a public verdict, what kind of operation is this? It is a political trial, a form of persecution to humiliate his character without reason,” she wrote.
Cheang added that as a member of Au’s family, she hoped she would be allowed to write to her husband and have regular visits that “would not be deprived by additional criteria”.
“As for other things, I believe all subjective wishes would only lead to greater disappointment, therefore I don’t wish to think or talk about them,” she wrote.
According to the court’s press release on Friday, Au’s family’s request for regular visits had been approved.

Au had been remanded in custody for more than a year since his arrest last July. Authorities said at the time that Au allegedly helped foreign organisations disseminate false information about Macau and arouse hatred among residents towards the government.
According to Macau police, Au was also suspected of having long-term contact with “multiple overseas anti-China entities”, disrupting the city’s 2024 chief executive election, and prompting foreign countries to take hostile actions against Macau.
His daughter reportedly said that Au had been denied phone calls and family visits, as well as access to a lawyer of his choosing.
Under Macau’s national security law, subversion of state power carries a sentence of 10 to 25 years in prison, while establishing links with foreign groups or individuals to endanger national security is punishable by three to 10 years.
The offence of violation of secrecy under Macau’s penal code carries a maximum sentence of one year.
Au, a pro-democracy politician who served as a lawmaker in the city’s Legislative Assembly for two decades until 2021, was a founding member of numerous opposition groups, including the New Democratic Macau Association.
He was also a founding member of the now-dissolved Macau Union of Democratic Development, which held annual candlelight vigils commemorating the Tiananmen Square crackdown until local authorities banned the event in 2021.

data.title: ‘Bullish on China’: US brand Levi’s bucks retail headwinds through localisation
data.description:
US apparel retailer Levi Strauss & Co says it is bullish on China and plans further investment and new store openings in the market, riding robust growth driven by young shoppers.
While the consumer market in China remains challenging for many multinationals, with a host of foreign brands shuttering stores amid rapid market shifts and broader consumption headwinds, Levi’s sees itself as an exception.
“We are going to be able to see China become a much bigger portion of our business globally,” the company’s executive vice-president and chief commercial officer, Gianluca Flore, said. “I’m aware of other brands, even luxury brands, that are reducing [their footprint]. I’m personally and professionally bullish on China.”
He added that Levi’s was a relatively small brand, macroeconomic shifts were not affecting it directly, and he believed the macroeconomic environment in China would eventually improve.
The company, headquartered in San Francisco, says its business outside North America makes up more than 60 per cent of its global business. Asia accounts for a relatively small share, but it says it views the region – and China in particular – as an important long-term growth opportunity.
In the third quarter, Levi’s net revenues in Asia rose 10 per cent year on year, marking the third straight quarter of double-digit growth, according to its quarterly earnings report.

Flore said the company’s performance in China had improved markedly in the past 12 months, and it had reset its expectations. He said Levi’s core consumer base in China was fashion-forward and trend-conscious, with an average age of 20 to 30.
He attributed the growth in China to a strategy that adopted a global framework but included strong local nuances in marketing and product offerings that were tailored to Chinese consumers.
“Within the global assortment, we have some fine tuning, some nuances that we bring to the products in certain cases,” Flore said. “We are really open, and we try ... to be flexible and agile to adapt to that nuance.”
He said the company followed a key city strategy that prioritised investment and marketing efforts in first-tier cities, while actively cooperating with local partners in operating some franchise stores.
Wang Tianshi, an analyst at the Shanghai-based LeadLeo Research Institute, said that foreign retailers seeking to gain a foothold in the Chinese market needed to “first flatten organisational structures”.
“Merchandising must cater closely to local niche preferences in China, reduce standard global sourcing and expand locally developed products,” Wang said. “Only by keeping pace with China’s fast-shifting consumption trends can foreign retailers turn their brand equity into sustainable competitive advantages.”

data.title: Overseas institutions keen on Hong Kong university towns, happy to help peers
data.description:
Leaders of overseas institutions have expressed keen interest in taking part in Hong Kong’s planned university towns in the Northern Metropolis megaproject and stress that while financing remains a challenge, they will collaborate on activities to help ensure projects are financially viable.
The university heads also called on the Hong Kong government to provide affordable housing in the new university towns, roll out policy incentives to retain top global talent and clearly define what success would look like for local and international partnerships.
More than 130 leaders from over 50 top universities across five continents visited the city this week for the two-day World Class University Presidents Forum 2026, hosted by Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.
In an interview, five of them expressed their interest in and views on the planned university towns in the Northern Metropolis, a megadevelopment near Hong Kong’s border with mainland China that aims to transform about 30,000 hectares (74,132 acres) of land into a technology hub and economic engine.
The government hopes the three self-financed university towns – with core campus areas totalling 300 hectares – will foster collaboration among industry, academia and research, and attract world-famous institutions and first-class scientific facilities.
Stuart Croft, vice-chancellor and president of Britain’s University of Warwick, said his institution was interested in establishing a presence in the university towns, which he described as a “triple helix” model in which universities, industry and the government drove new economic growth.

However, he said overseas universities would not work independently in the university towns or take the lead, but would choose instead to partner with local institutions.
“When Hong Kong universities are engaged in the process, we’d be happy to have conversations about what we might be able to do to help support [it]. But we’re not in a leadership position in that context,” he said.
“The responsible institution for working [out] how it will be financed has to be the Hong Kong university, not the partner university. Of course, we will need to have activities together that make the finances work, but we will not be in charge of putting together those measures.”




The University of Manchester was interested in the project as it had already had deep partnerships in Hong Kong for many years, president and vice-chancellor Duncan Ivison said, while conceding that financing was always a challenge.
Secretary for Education Christine Choi Yuk-lin said last month that overseas universities had told the authorities that the substantial infrastructure investment remained their greatest challenge, given that the towns had adopted a self-financing model for development.
She said she expected them to take part in the university towns via joint programmes, joint laboratories, research collaborations and academic exchanges in the short term.
Joan Guardia, rector of the University of Barcelona in Spain, and Stephen McArthur, principal and vice-chancellor of the University of Strathclyde in Britain, both said they were interested in exploring international partnerships.
They are not the only universities eyeing the project. A prestigious university in mainland China has already lined up the city’s oldest university to join the race.
On Monday, the University of Hong Kong announced that it and Peking University in Beijing would actively explore establishing a joint centre in the Northern Metropolis.
Looking ahead, the overseas university heads called on the Hong Kong government to provide more support and clarity on the collaboration.

Mosa Moshabela, vice-chancellor and principal of the University of Cape Town in South Africa, urged local authorities to define from the outset what “success” would look like for collaborations with international institutions, and to clarify what was expected of overseas partner institutions.
He added that affordable housing should be integrated into the university towns to attract talent.
Warwick’s Croft said that while universities were powerful magnets for talent, success would still depend on the retention measures the government was able to offer and implement.
“It’s then up to governments whether they allow them to stay, whether they give them incentives to stay, because great talent can move,” he said.
There are three planned university towns in the Northern Metropolis: the 26-hectare Hung Shui Kiu university town; the 100-hectare San Tin university town; and the 180-hectare Ta Kwu Ling university town.
The first batch of land in Hung Shui Kiu, about five hectares, will be formed by the end of this year. Universities wishing to establish a presence in Hung Shui Kiu must submit their proposals by the end of next month.
The government earmarked a HK$10 billion loan scheme for the Hung Shui Kiu university town.
Institutions setting foot in the towns will be required to focus on cutting-edge scientific research and collaborate with local industries on curriculum development, teaching and learning, internships and applied research to cultivate talent.
They will also have to partner with renowned mainland and overseas institutions, strengthen linkages and collaboration with leading enterprises and develop shared facilities.
According to the government plan, institutions may construct permanent premises to expand their capacity, reprovision existing campuses and provide or enhance teaching and ancillary facilities, including libraries, laboratories, student guidance centres, research facilities and student hostels.

data.title: Hong Kong police to enable AI facial recognition on CCTV network this month
data.description:
Hong Kong police will enable artificial intelligence-powered facial recognition technology across their expanding smart surveillance network this month to improve the tracking of missing persons or suspects, with plans to save the data it generates for up to 180 days.
The force said the facial recognition technology was widely used by law enforcement agencies around the world and stressed that residents’ privacy rights would be protected.
“Leveraging AI [facial recognition] would cut the time we spend reviewing the closed-circuit television [CCTV] footage to track down target persons,” Eric Leung Ming-leung, senior superintendent of the force’s operations wing, said.
“This technology will speed up the initial review and free our officers for other investigative work.”
Leung said that tracking missing persons or suspects often tied up many patrol officers. Facial recognition was akin to having extra officers who could search around the clock to locate those people more efficiently, he added.
He said the facial recognition technology in the “SmartView” surveillance camera installation programme would work in two ways.
Officers could input a suspect’s facial features and ask the system to check whether the person had appeared in specific footage or on certain cameras within a given time frame, allowing them to review the person’s movements.
The second function would operate in real time. For example, Leung said that if an elderly person went missing and could not be traced in past footage, their facial features could be entered into the system, which would then send an alert about when and where the person appeared on camera for police to follow up.

He stressed that searches in the system would require approval from an officer at the inspector level or above and must be aligned with the goals of safeguarding national security, preventing and detecting crime and ensuring public safety.
Officers would also have to justify their use of the system, such as how many cameras and how much footage they needed to review, and whether that scope was proportionate to their investigation, Leung said.
The officer who approved the search would then check whether the search had gone beyond the approved scope or strayed from its original purpose, he added.
In terms of data storage, Leung said police had to comply with the relevant ordinance and that storing the footage was costly, so data should not be kept for more than 31 days to balance operational needs with resources.
However, data generated by the facial recognition function could be retained for longer as it occupied less storage space than video footage, he said.
The force said it planned to keep relevant data, such as when and where a person appeared in footage, for no more than 180 days.
“We think that if we can keep the data longer, it will be better for our investigation,” Leung said.
“Some cases took place six months or even a year ago, so the longer the data is kept, the better it will be for us.”
The force stated that all CCTV cameras installed under the SmartView project captured only public areas, and that all operating procedures were based on independent privacy impact assessments and discussions with the Office of the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data (PCPD), to ensure residents’ privacy rights were protected.
In response to South China Morning Post queries, the PCPD said it would not comment on individual cases, but that all data users were required to comply with the requirements of the Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance and its relevant data protection principles when they collected, held, processed or used personal data in Hong Kong, regardless of whether facial recognition technology was involved.
“From time to time, the PCPD provides our observations and views from the perspective of protecting personal data privacy to government departments and bureaus on their new initiatives or proposals to facilitate compliance with the requirements of the [ordinance],” the privacy watchdog added.
The SmartView project, first rolled out in 2024, included plans to install 60,000 cameras across the city by 2028.
Leung said SmartView had already used AI for people counting and automatic licence plate recognition. As of the end of October, the system had helped police solve 2,192 criminal cases, including murder, arson and theft, and arrest 2,831 people.
In the first phase, Leung said police had focused on cameras operated by government departments and public organisations, and they would expand the initiative to private organisations in the next phase, starting from locations with higher pedestrian flows, such as shopping centres and transitional housing.
Police had talked with several shopping centres about linking their cameras to the system, he said, adding that the response had been positive and the first batch could be connected as early as the end of this year.
Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung previously said that authorities were still considering whether to put up additional notices telling the public that a shopping centre’s cameras had been linked to the police system, arguing it “may not be necessary” as many malls had already displayed recording notices.
Leung said police encouraged the shopping centres to put up notifications, as the system gave the public much confidence.
“If people know the shopping centre is working with us, they will feel safer, which could have a positive impact on its business.”

“At the start of Trump’s second term, many wondered whether Elon Musk would play a moderating role in the White House’s approach to China,” Chan said. “After the Busan agreement, there seems to be less of a role for someone like Musk to play in US-China relations.”
Bai said Musk’s value as a diplomatic conduit had diminished.
“Musk himself has gone from being a ‘strategic bridge’ to just one of the American businessmen Beijing can engage with,” he said.
Ultimately, however, Trump remains in the Oval Office for the next two years, holding executive veto power and agency leadership that could shield Musk from major regulatory challenges. But the days of unfettered access may be over.
“My guess is Musk will keep a lower political profile for a while to draw less attention to his businesses,” Kollar said.
“There will likely be increased congressional scrutiny, but without executive action, I’d be surprised if he changed his merger plans or how Tesla operates in China.”

data.title: Hong Kong prisoner support group operator arrested over alleged seditious books
data.description:
Hong Kong national security police have arrested an operator of a local prisoner support group on suspicion of importing seditious publications, days after the group revealed that customs had seized dozens of books it had ordered from Taiwan.
Police said officers carried out an enforcement operation in Mong Kok on Thursday morning, arresting a local man, 34, on suspicion of “importing a publication that has a seditious intention”, an offence under the Safeguarding National Security Ordinance.
The suspect, the director of a local company, was understood to be the person in charge of Waiting Bird, an advocacy group focused on prisoner welfare.
Investigations showed that the man was suspected of importing seditious books in October to sell at local bookstores.
The books were allegedly intended to incite hatred, contempt or disaffection against the central authorities and the Hong Kong government.
Acting under a court warrant, officers searched the man’s home and the company’s premises, seizing digital devices used to buy the books, documents and other publications deemed seditious.
The suspect remained in custody for questioning on Thursday evening.




The arrest came after Waiting Bird announced on its social media page on Monday that more than 60 books it had ordered went missing in a shipment from Taiwan last month. The group said the books, comprising four titles, were related to Hong Kong.
According to the group, the consignment was initially scheduled to arrive on October 13 but was delivered on October 20.
The logistics company handling the delivery told the group that the goods had been inspected by customs and that the shipment arrived with more than 60 volumes missing.
The firm also provided a notice from the Customs and Excise Department indicating that officers had executed the seizure under the national security legal framework.
Under local legislation, enforcement officers are empowered to seize articles reasonably suspected of having a seditious intention, regardless of whether any arrests have been made.
Waiting Bird earlier said the department had issued a brief written reply confirming that the missing books had been seized, although it did not detail the specific grounds for the move.
“We do not believe the seized books carry any seditious intention, and they should be returned,” the group said in its Monday statement.
The group noted that the seized titles were not new releases and had previously been imported from Taiwan and sold at an affiliated shop and other independent bookstores in Hong Kong without any issues.
“We have neither the intention nor the ability to endanger national security,” the group said.
“We will continue to adhere to this principle, accompanying everyone through this era within legal boundaries.”
A customs spokesman earlier said he would not comment on individual cases. He said the department would detain items suspected of having a seditious intention in accordance with the law and that customs would refer cases to the force’s National Security Department for follow-up action where appropriate.
Waiting Bird was founded in 2022 by former Yau Tsim Mong district councillor Derek Chu Kong-wai, a veteran labour and grassroots community organiser.
Chu was arrested in 2023 on suspicion of promoting Mandatory Provident Fund schemes without registration. He was released on bail without charge at the time.
